title: Sell Mineral Rights in Gaines County, TX/NM
metaTitle: Sell Mineral Rights in Gaines County, TX | Royalty Buyer
metaDescription: Gaines County has quietly become one of the busiest counties in the Midland Basin. See how royalty and mineral interests get priced here, straight talk.
heroLead: Gaines County doesn't get the headlines Midland or Reeves does, but the well density out here has quietly become some of the heaviest in the entire basin.
intro: I remember when Gaines County was considered a secondary target compared to the core Midland Basin counties, mostly Spraberry and San Andres vertical production with limited horizontal interest. That changed hard once operators proved out the Wolfcamp across the county, and Seminole and Denver City became staging points for a level of pad development that surprised a lot of people who'd written the county off.

If you own royalty or minerals in Gaines County, the sheer density of current drilling means your interest is worth a careful, specific look rather than a rough guess, and that's what I do before I ever put a number in front of an owner.

sections.heading: One of the most heavily permitted counties around
paragraphs: Gaines County has consistently ranked among the busiest counties in Texas for new drilling permits over the past several years, with multiple large public operators running dense multi-well pad programs across both the Midland and Delaware-adjacent portions of the county. That density matters for mineral owners because it means the odds of continued development on or near your tract are genuinely high, not speculative.

The county also straddles a transition zone where Midland Basin characteristics start giving way to Delaware Basin geology further west, which is part of why some Gaines County acreage gets priced more aggressively than you'd expect from a county that used to be considered secondary.

sections.heading: Seminole, Denver City, and the acreage around them
paragraphs: Seminole serves as the county seat and the main service hub, while Denver City on the western edge has become a real staging point for drilling activity pushing toward the New Mexico line. Minerals near either town tend to sit closer to active pad development than acreage in the more rural stretches between them, which factors into how I underwrite risk on undeveloped or lightly developed tracts.

If you're not sure exactly where your tract sits relative to current drilling, send me the legal description or section and block, and I'll pull permitting activity in that specific area rather than quoting a county-wide average that doesn't reflect your actual acreage.

sections.heading: What moves the number for your specific interest
paragraphs: Net royalty acres, decline stage of any producing wells, and nearby permitted-but-undrilled locations are the three biggest inputs, and in Gaines County that third factor carries unusual weight given how much permitting activity is happening county-wide right now. Values here vary with commodity pricing and proximity to the busiest development corridors, so I build a range specific to your tract rather than quoting a flat multiple.

If your check has been climbing recently because a new well came online nearby, that's useful information rather than background noise, and I'll want to see it. Recent production trends tell me more about future value than a single month's number in isolation.

sections.heading: Family land, heirs, and getting this right
paragraphs: A lot of Gaines County mineral ownership traces back to farming and ranching families who held onto minerals across generations, and it's common for an interest to now be split among several heirs, some of whom may not even know they own anything. If that's your situation, I can generally work with your individual share without requiring the rest of the family to be involved.

This isn't tax or legal advice, and for questions about estate division or the tax treatment of a sale, talk to your CPA or attorney. What I can promise is a straightforward, honest number built off real data, and no pressure if you decide to hold.

sections.heading: How a Gaines County closing usually goes
paragraphs: Once we settle on a number, I put together a purchase and sale agreement and run title work to confirm your interest matches county and state records. Most clean-title closings in Gaines County run three to six weeks from signature to funds.

If probate or a missing heir is holding things up, I can usually still get the deal structured, it just takes longer, and I'll explain exactly what curative work is needed for your specific chain of title before you decide whether to move forward.

faqs.question: Why is Gaines County getting so much drilling activity lately?
faqs.answer: The Wolfcamp proved out well across much of the county, and its position between the Midland and Delaware basins gives operators strong economics on both conventional and stacked lateral development. That's driven permit counts up significantly in recent years.

faqs.question: Does it matter whether my Gaines County acreage is near Seminole or Denver City?
faqs.answer: It can influence how close your tract sits to current active development, which affects how I weigh future drilling potential against current production in building your offer.

faqs.question: My royalty check has been going up, does that mean my interest is worth more now?
faqs.answer: Often yes, if the increase reflects a new well coming online on your unit rather than a temporary price spike. Send me a few recent check stubs so I can see the actual trend across several months rather than a single one.

faqs.question: Do you buy interests in Gaines County that don't currently produce anything?
faqs.answer: Yes, though the offer reflects the speculative nature of undeveloped acreage rather than current cash flow. Given how active permitting is county-wide, undeveloped Gaines County minerals still carry real, if different, value.
